In [[probability theory]], it is possible to approximate the [[moment (mathematics)|moments]], such as the mean <math>\mu = \operatorname{E}\left[X\right]</math> and variance <math>\sigma^2 = \operatorname{var}\left[X\right]</math>, of a function ''f'' of a [[random variable]] ''X'' using [[Taylor expansion]]s, provided that ''f'' is sufficiently differentiable and that the moments of ''X'' are finite. 

==First moment==
A Taylor expansion of the [[expected value]] of <math>f(X)</math> can be found via:<ref name="Benaroya">Haym Benaroya, Seon Mi Han, and Mark Nagurka. ''Probability Models in Engineering and Science''. CRC Press, 2005, p166.</ref>

: <math>
\begin{align}
\operatorname{E}\left[f(X)\right] & {} = \operatorname{E}\left[f\left(\mu_X + \left(X - \mu_X\right)\right)\right] \\
& {} \approx \operatorname{E}\left[f(\mu_X) + f'(\mu_X)\left(X-\mu_X\right) + \frac{1}{2}f''(\mu_X) \left(X - \mu_X\right)^2 \right] \\
& {} = f(\mu_X) + f'(\mu_X) \operatorname{E} \left[ X-\mu_X \right] + \frac{1}{2}f''(\mu_X) \operatorname{E} \left[ \left(X - \mu_X\right)^2 \right].
\end{align}
</math>

Since <math>E[X-\mu_X]=0,</math> the second term vanishes. Also, <math>E[(X-\mu_X)^2]</math> is <math>\sigma_X^2</math>. Therefore,

:<math>\operatorname{E}\left[f(X)\right]\approx f(\mu_X) +\frac{f''(\mu_X)}{2}\sigma_X^2</math>.

So, the output expected value is seen to depend on the input variance.

==Second moment==
Similarly, the variance is obtained as:<ref name="Benaroya"/>

:<math>\operatorname{var}\left[f(X)\right]\approx \left(f'(\operatorname{E}\left[X\right])\right)^2\operatorname{var}\left[X\right] + \frac{\left(f''(\operatorname{E}\left[X\right])\right)^2}{2}\left(\operatorname{var}\left[X\right]\right)^2 = \left(f'(\mu_X)\right)^2\sigma^2_X -\frac{1}{4}\left(f''(\mu_X)\right)^2\sigma_X^4</math>

It improves on the typical first-order approximation, which will be a poor approximation if <math>f(X)</math> is highly non-linear (see [[uncertainty propagation]]):

:<math>\operatorname{var}\left[f(X)\right]\approx \left(f'(\operatorname{E}\left[X\right])\right)^2\operatorname{var}\left[X\right]</math>

A third order approximation, when X follows a [[normal distribution]], is:<ref name="HendebyGustafsson">{{cite web|last1=Hendeby|first1=Gustaf|last2=Gustafsson|first2=Fredrik|title=ON NONLINEAR TRANSFORMATIONS OF GAUSSIAN DISTRIBUTIONS|url=http://users.isy.liu.se/en/rt/fredrik/reports/07SSPut.pdf|access-date=5 October 2017}}</ref>

:<math>\operatorname{var}\left[f(X)\right]\approx = \left(f'(\mu_X)\right)^2\sigma^2_X + \frac{1}{2}\left(f''(\mu_X)\right)^2\sigma_X^4 + \left(f'(\mu_X)\right)\left(f'''(\mu_X)\right)\sigma_X^4</math>

==Random vectors==
If ''X'' is a [[Multivariate random variable|random vector]], the approximations for the mean and variance of <math>f(X)</math> are given by<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Rego |first=Bruno V. |last2=Weiss |first2=Dar |last3=Bersi |first3=Matthew R. |last4=Humphrey |first4=Jay D. |date=14 December 2021 |title=Uncertainty quantification in subject‐specific estimation of local vessel mechanical properties |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/cnm.3535 |journal=[[International Journal for Numerical Methods in Biomedical Engineering]] |language=en |volume=37 |issue=12 |article-number=e3535 |doi=10.1002/cnm.3535 |issn=2040-7939 |pmc=9019846 |pmid=34605615}}</ref>
: <math>
\begin{align}
\operatorname{E}(f(X)) &= f(\mu_X) + \frac{1}{2} \operatorname{trace}(H_f(\mu_X) \Sigma_X) \\
\operatorname{var}(f(X)) &= \nabla f(\mu_X)^t \Sigma_X \nabla f(\mu_X) + \frac{1}{2} \operatorname{trace} \left( H_f(\mu_X) \Sigma_X H_f(\mu_X) \Sigma_X \right).
\end{align}
</math>
Here <math>\nabla f</math> and <math>H_f</math> denote the [[gradient]] and the [[Hessian matrix]] respectively, and <math> \Sigma_X </math> is the [[covariance matrix]] of ''X''.

==Multiple variables==

It is possible to generalize this to functions of more than one variable using [[Taylor expansion#Taylor series in several variables|multivariate Taylor expansions]]. For example (see [[ratio distribution]]),<ref name="RatioMoments" />

:<math>\operatorname{E}\left[\frac{X}{Y}\right]\approx\frac{\operatorname{E}\left[X\right]}{\operatorname{E}\left[Y\right]} -\frac{\operatorname{cov}\left[X,Y\right]}{\operatorname{E}\left[Y\right]^2}+\frac{\operatorname{E}\left[X\right]}{\operatorname{E}\left[Y\right]^3}\operatorname{var}\left[Y\right]</math>

With <math> f(X) = g(X)^2 </math>, we get <math>\operatorname{E}\left[Y^2\right]</math>. The variance is then computed using the formula 
<math>\operatorname{var}\left[Y\right] = \operatorname{E}\left[Y^2\right] - \mu_Y^2</math>.  

An example is,<ref name="RatioMoments">{{cite journal |last1=van Kempen |first1=G.m.p. |last2=van Vliet |first2=L.j. |title=Mean and Variance of Ratio Estimators Used in Fluorescence Ratio Imaging |journal=Cytometry |date=1 April 2000 |volume=39 |issue=4 |pages=300-305 |doi=10.1002/(SICI)1097-0320(20000401)39:4<300::AID-CYTO8>3.0.CO;2-O |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1002/%28SICI%291097-0320%2820000401%2939%3A4%3C300%3A%3AAID-CYTO8%3E3.0.CO%3B2-O |access-date=2024-08-14|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

:<math>\operatorname{var}\left[\frac{X}{Y}\right]\approx\frac{\operatorname{var}\left[X\right]}{\operatorname{E}\left[Y\right]^2}-\frac{2\operatorname{E}\left[X\right]}{\operatorname{E}\left[Y\right]^3}\operatorname{cov}\left[X,Y\right]+\frac{\operatorname{E}\left[X\right]^2}{\operatorname{E}\left[Y\right]^4}\operatorname{var}\left[Y\right].</math>

===First product moment===
To find a second-order approximation for the covariance of functions of two random variables (with the same function applied to both), one can proceed as follows. First, note that <math>\operatorname{cov}\left[f(X),f(Y)\right]=\operatorname{E}\left[f(X)f(Y)\right]-\operatorname{E}\left[f(X)\right]\operatorname{E}\left[f(Y)\right]</math>. Since a second-order expansion for <math>\operatorname{E}\left[f(X)\right]</math> has already been derived above, it only remains to find <math>\operatorname{E}\left[f(X)f(Y)\right]</math>. Treating <math>f(X)f(Y)</math> as a two-variable function, the second-order Taylor expansion is as follows:

: <math>
\begin{align}
f(X)f(Y) & {} \approx f(\mu_X) f(\mu_Y) + (X-\mu_X) f'(\mu_X)f(\mu_Y) + (Y - \mu_Y)f(\mu_X)f'(\mu_Y) + \frac{1}{2}\left[(X-\mu_X)^2 f''(\mu_X)f(\mu_Y) + 2(X-\mu_X)(Y-\mu_Y)f'(\mu_X)f'(\mu_Y) + (Y-\mu_Y)^2 f(\mu_X)f''(\mu_Y) \right]
\end{align}
</math>

Taking expectation of the above and simplifying—making use of the identities <math>\operatorname{E}(X^2)=\operatorname{var}(X)+\left[\operatorname{E}(X)\right]^2</math> and <math>\operatorname{E}(XY)=\operatorname{cov}(X,Y)+\left[\operatorname{E}(X)\right]\left[\operatorname{E}(Y)\right]</math>—leads to <math>\operatorname{E}\left[f(X)f(Y)\right]\approx f(\mu_X)f(\mu_Y)+f'(\mu_X)f'(\mu_Y)\operatorname{cov}(X,Y)+\frac{1}{2}f''(\mu_X)f(\mu_Y)\operatorname{var}(X)+\frac{1}{2}f(\mu_X)f''(\mu_Y)\operatorname{var}(Y)</math>. Hence,

: <math>
\begin{align}
\operatorname{cov}\left[f(X),f(Y)\right] & {} \approx f(\mu_X)f(\mu_Y)+f'(\mu_X)f'(\mu_Y)\operatorname{cov}(X,Y)+\frac{1}{2}f''(\mu_X)f(\mu_Y)\operatorname{var}(X)+\frac{1}{2}f(\mu_X)f''(\mu_Y)\operatorname{var}(Y) - \left[f(\mu_X)+\frac{1}{2}f''(\mu_X)\operatorname{var}(X)\right] \left[f(\mu_Y)+\frac{1}{2}f''(\mu_Y)\operatorname{var}(Y) \right] \\
& {} = f'(\mu_X)f'(\mu_Y) \operatorname{cov}(X,Y) - \frac{1}{4}f''(\mu_X)f''(\mu_Y)\operatorname{var}(X)\operatorname{var}(Y)
\end{align}
</math>
